analysis.one_liner: Creates a temporary federal reinsurance fund to keep terrorism insurance available after 9/11.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the Senate two months after 9/11, the bill was referred to the Commerce Committee and never received a vote or a markup.
analysis.plain_summary: After the September 11 attacks, insurers faced the largest losses in their history and began pulling back from writing terrorism coverage, which threatened loans and leases for buildings and businesses. This bill would have created a National Terrorism Reinsurance Fund at the Commerce Department, backed by up to $50 billion in Treasury loans, to pay a share of terrorism claims above what each insurer retains. In exchange, insurers would have been required to cover terrorism in their property and casualty policies, barred from passing through more than their actual assessments as surcharges, and required to justify any terrorism-related rate increases to state regulators and the FTC.
analysis.who_benefits: Building owners, businesses, and homebuyers who needed terrorism coverage to close deals or obtain mortgages and leases, since insurers had stopped offering it or priced it out of reach. Insurers also benefit: the federal government backs their terrorism losses above 10 percent of their premium base, with 70 to 90 percent reimbursement, and the federal backstop caps their worst-case exposure.

how_it_helps.text: The Fund would reimburse insurers for 70 to 90 percent of terrorism losses above a 10 percent retention, drawing on Treasury loans up to $50 billion, and pay 90 percent of covered losses between $50 billion and $100 billion directly from the Treasury in 2002. [S3]

Insurers would be required to cover terrorism losses with the same deductibles and terms as ordinary perils, and barred from denying or canceling coverage solely because of terrorism risk, guaranteeing availability for policyholders. [S3]

Insurers could only surcharge policyholders for the premiums and assessments they actually owed into the Fund, had to file reports justifying terrorism-related rate increases, and the FTC and GAO would review insurer rates and claims for unfair practices. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers ultimately stand behind the Fund: the Treasury lends up to $50 billion (with direct payments up to $100 billion in catastrophic years), and taxpayers bear the residual risk if claims outrun the premiums insurers pay in. Policyholders pay a terrorism surcharge passed through by insurers, and the bill preempts state rate and form regulation on covered contracts.

drawbacks.text: The Fund's premiums, assessments, and loans are repayable only up to the limits set, and in a catastrophic year the Treasury would pay 90 percent of losses above $50 billion out of general revenues, so taxpayers carry a large residual risk if another major attack occurs. [S3]

The bill preempts state laws on insurance rates, policy forms, financial requirements, and licensing for Fund contracts, and exempts the Fund and the surcharges from federal, state, and local taxes, stripping state regulators of their usual authority over the participating market. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: At the time, the private terrorism insurance market had effectively shut down, and the bill's mandatory coverage plus federal backstop would have restored coverage at a controlled cost, with rate controls preventing insurers from using the program to overcharge. The offsetting cost is the transfer of catastrophic tail risk to taxpayers and the preemption of state regulation, a trade-off later resolved in a different form when Congress passed a terrorism risk program with a larger federal share and fewer rate protections in 2002.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate in late November 2001, referred to the Commerce Committee, and never came up for a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Hollings introduced the bill on November 29, 2001, with Sens. Boxer and Wyden as cosponsors, and it was read twice and referred to the Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee. [S5][S4]
No further action was taken after referral; the bill never received a markup or a floor vote, and the Congress ended January 3, 2003. [S5] [S1]
Congress instead enacted the Terrorism Risk Insurance Act of 2002, a federal terrorism reinsurance backstop with a larger federal share and fewer rate controls than this bill proposed.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Taxpayers were spared the $50 billion-plus contingent liability this bill would have created, while the property-casualty industry, having pressed for a federal backstop after 9/11, ultimately got one under TRIA with weaker rate and surcharge limits than Hollings' bill would have imposed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers spared liability; insurers got backstop later

for.name: Sen. Ernest Hollings
for.role: Chair, Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the National Terrorism Reinsurance Fund Act and championed a federal backstop with rate controls.

for.name: Sens. Barbara Boxer and Ron Wyden

against.name: Senate Commerce Committee majority
against.role: Held the bill without a markup or vote
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to a markup or reported it to the floor.

against.name: Insurance industry
against.role: Property-casualty insurers and reinsurers seeking a federal backstop
against.what_they_did: Favored federal terrorism reinsurance after 9/11 but opposed the bill's mandatory coverage and rate-control provisions; the final TRIA reflected their preferences.

sides.party_line_note: Both cosponsors were Democrats, but the bill died in a committee without a recorded vote, leaving no roll-call record of partisan positions.

industries.note: The bill would have capped insurers' terrorism losses at a 10 percent retention with the federal government covering 70 to 90 percent above that, but it also mandated terrorism coverage, limited surcharges to actual assessments, and subjected insurers to FTC and GAO review. Insurers got the backstop they wanted without those limits when TRIA passed instead.
A federal Fund would have competed with private reinsurers for terrorism risk, reducing their market, though it also stabilized the property-casualty market they serve.
Without terrorism coverage, leases and construction loans were stalling after 9/11; a federal backstop would have restored the coverage those deals required.

The bill preempts state rate, form, financial, and licensing law for Fund contracts, shrinking regulators' authority over the covered market while requiring them to certify insurer capacity and report rate filings.

Policyholders get guaranteed terrorism coverage and surcharge limits; taxpayers carry the residual catastrophic risk above the Fund's resources, up to direct Treasury payments on losses between $50 billion and $100 billion.
